Chapter 8: Renormalization

8 Renormalization

“The shell game that we play … is technically called ‘renormalization’. But no matter how clever the word, it is still what I would call a dippy process! Having to resort to such hocus-pocus has prevented us from proving that the theory of quantum electrodynamics is mathematically self-consistent. It’s surprising that the theory still hasn’t been proved self-consistent one way or the other by now; I suspect that renormalization is not mathematically legitimate.”

— Richard Feynman

8.1 Stereotypical Examples of (Counterterm) Renormalization

  • Renormalization is the process of removing infinities by putting them in “bare” variables

  • The three most stereotypical examples of renormalization of quantum electrodynamics (and in general) are the following

    1. Vacuum Polarization
    2. Electron Self Interaction
    3. The anomalous magnetic moment

  • There are two types of renorormalization:

    1. Counterterm renormalization

    2. Wilsonian renormalization

      • Arguably the coolest type of renormalization but it seems like it’s completely different than traditional counterterm renormalization

8.1.1 Mass Renormalization

  • This is equivalent to the Electron self interaction

Why Renormalize?

  • In general, divergences form due to loop diagrams which give infinite integrals

Definition 8.1.1.1 (Superficial Degree of Divergence).

  • This quantity is a very standard quantity which counts essentially how bady something diverges.

    • In QED, define the following quantities :

      𝑁𝑒=#︎elec𝑁𝛾=#︎phot𝑃𝑒=#︎electron prop.𝑃𝛾=#︎photon prop.𝑉=#︎vertices𝐿=#︎loops
  • The degree of divergence is 𝐷=4𝐿−𝑃𝑒−2𝑃𝛾=2(𝑃𝑒+𝑃𝛾−𝑉+1)−𝑃𝑒−2𝑃𝛾
  • Now we will make sense of this quantity

Definition 8.1.1.2 (PV Regulation).

  • Consider a divergent integral, such as

    ∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)41𝑘2

    . The superficial degree of divergence is the difference in powers of 𝑘 in the numerator and denominator.

    • That is, 𝐷ex.=2.

  • PV regulation works by giving the integral a cutoff

    ∫Λd4𝑘(2𝜋)41𝑘2∝Λ2
  • We would then enter counterterms into the lagrangian which would precisely (or not so precisely in some schemes like MS‾ as you will see) cancel them out

  • Now we see that, in fact, the degree of divergence counts the power of Λ. If 𝐷=0, it is proportional to lnΛ

  • There is also another way to evaluate the integrals which shows us a divergence

Definition 8.1.1.3 (DimReg).

  • DimReg (dimension regulation) is a method of scanning for divergences by setting 𝑑=4−𝜀 and taking lim𝜀→0of the integral

    • You only take this limit after you subtract the divergence

  • Lets look at the actual electron self energy to see what we can analyze

  • At 1 loop,

    ⟨Ω|𝑇𝜓̄(𝑥)𝜓(𝑥)|Ω⟩=feynman diagrams=normal electron propagator+momentum integral of some function 𝑓

  • We define

    𝑓≡𝑖(𝑝+𝑚)𝑝2−𝑚02+𝑖0(−Σ2(𝑝))𝑖(𝑝+𝑚0)𝑝2−𝑚02+𝑖0

  • Essentially, we want to evaluate the loop integral given by

    𝑖𝜎2(𝑝)=(−𝑖𝑒)2∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)4𝛾𝜇𝑖(𝑘+𝑚0)𝑘2−𝑚02+𝑖0𝛾𝜈−𝑖𝑔𝜇𝜈(𝑝−𝑘)2+𝑖0

  • This trick that we use to evaluate these integrals is called feynman paramaterization

  • Notice that

    1𝐴𝐵=∫01d𝑥1(𝑥𝐴+(1−𝑥)𝐵)2

  • Taking 𝐴=(𝑝−𝑚0)2−𝑚02+𝑖0 and 𝐵=𝑘2−𝑚02+𝑖0, we obtain that

    1𝐴𝐵=∫01d𝑥1[𝑥2−2𝑥𝑘·𝑝+𝑥𝑝2−𝑥𝜇2−(1−𝑥)𝑚02+𝑖𝜖+𝑥2𝑝2−𝑥2𝑝2]2

8.1.2 Vacuum Polarization

  • This is the photon splitting into an electron and a positron and then them combining again into a photon

  • The vertex evaluates to

    feyn diag=−(−𝑖𝑒)2∫d4𝑘(2𝜋)4𝑖(𝑝−𝑘)2−𝑚2𝑖𝑘2−𝑚2×Tr[𝛾𝜇(𝑘−𝑝+𝑚)𝛾𝜈(𝑘+𝑚)]
    tr[𝛾𝜇(𝑘−𝑝+𝑚)𝛾𝜈(𝑘+𝑚)]=4[−𝑝𝜇𝑘𝜈−𝑘𝜇𝑝𝜈+2𝑘𝜇𝑘𝜈+𝑔𝜇𝜈(−𝑘2+𝑝·𝑘+𝑚2)]

  • We define the loop in this diagram as

    𝑖Π2𝜇𝜈≡∫𝑑4𝑘(2𝜋)4𝑖(𝑝−𝑘)2−𝑚2𝑖𝑘2−𝑚2×Tr[𝛾𝜇(𝑘−𝑝+𝑚)𝛾𝜈(𝑘+𝑚)]

  • With our trace, we get

    𝑖Π2𝜇𝜈=−4𝑒2∫𝑑4𝑘2𝑘𝜇𝑘𝜈+𝑔𝜇𝜈(−𝑘2+𝑝·𝑘+𝑚2)[(𝑝−𝑘)2−𝑚2+𝑖𝜖][𝑘2−𝑚2+𝑖𝜖]

  • We can parametrize this using a trick called feynman parameterization where we take 𝑘𝜇→𝑘𝜇+𝑝𝜇(1−𝑥) and integrate

Π2𝜇𝜈=4𝑖𝑒2∫𝑑4𝑘∫01𝑑𝑥2𝑘𝜇𝑘𝜈−𝑔𝜇𝜈[𝑘2−𝑥(1−𝑥)𝑝2−𝑚2][𝑘2+𝑝2𝑥(1−𝑥)−𝑚2]2=−8𝑝2𝑔𝜇𝜈𝑒2(4𝜋)𝑑/2Γ(2−𝑑/2)𝜇4−𝑑×∫01𝑑𝑥𝑥(1−𝑥)(1𝑚2−𝑝2𝑥(1−𝑥))2−𝑑/2

  • This yields

    Π2𝜇𝜈=−𝑒22𝜋2𝑝2𝑔𝜇𝜈∫01𝑑𝑥𝑥(1−𝑥)[2𝜖+ln(𝜇̃2𝑚2−𝑝2𝑥(1−𝑥))+𝑂(𝜖)]
